The priest of Jupiter, whose temple was in front of dem city, bring oxen and garlands to the gates, and would have made a sacrifice along with the plenty people.
But when the apostles, Barnabas and Paul, heard of it, dem tore dem clothes, and sprang into the plenty people, crying out,

“Men, why are you doing these things? We also are men of like passions with you, and bring you better news, that you should turn from these vain things to the living God, who made the sky, the earth, the sea, and all that is in dem;
who in the generations gone by allowed all the nations to walk in dem own ways.
Yet he didn’t leave imself without witness, in that he did good and give you rains from the sky and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with chop and gladness.”
Even saying these things, dem hardly stopped the plenty people from making a sacrifice to dem.
But some Jews from Antioch and Iconium come there, and having persuaded the plenty people, dem stoned Paul, and dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead.
But as the disciples stood around him, he rose up, and entered into the city. On the next day he go out with Barnabas to Derbe.
When dem had preached the Better news to that city, and had made many disciples, dem come back to Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch,
confirming the souls of the disciples, exhorting dem to continue in the faith, and that through many afflictions we must enter into God’s Kingdom.
When dem had appointed elders for dem in every assembly, and had prayed with fasting, dem commended dem to the Lord, on whom dem had believe.
Dem passed through Pisidia, and come to Pamphylia.
When dem had spoken the word in Perga, dem go down to Attalia.
From there dem sailed to Antioch, from where dem Bin dey committed to the grace of God for the work which dem had fulfilled.
When dem had arrived, and had gathered the assembly together, dem reported all the things that God had done with dem, and that he had opened a door of faith to the nations.
Dem stayed there with the disciples for a long time.
Some men come down from Judea and taught the brothers, “Unless You be circumcised after the custom of Moses, you no fit be saved.”
So when Paul and Barnabas had no small discord and discussion with dem, dem appointed Paul and Barnabas, and some others of dem, to go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and elders about this question.
Dem, being sent on dem way by the assembly, passed through both Phoenicia and Samaria, declaring the conversion of the Gentiles. Dem caused great gladness to all the brothers.
When dem had come to Jerusalem, dem were received by the assembly and the apostles and the elders, and dem reported all things that God had done with dem.
But some of the sect of the Pharisees who believe rose up, saying, “It is necessary to circumcise dem, and to command dem to keep the law of Moses.”
The apostles and the elders were gathered together to see about this matter.

When there Bin dey much discussion, Peter rose up and talk say to dem, “Brothers, you know that a good while ago God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the nations should hear the word of the Better news, and believe.
God, wey know the heart, testified about dem, giving dem the Holy Spirit, just like he did to us.
He made no distinction between us and dem, cleansing dem hearts by faith.
Now so why do you tempt God, that you should put a yoke on the neck of the disciples which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?
But we believe that We be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as Dem be.”
All the plenty people kept silence, and dem listened to Barnabas and Paul reporting what signs and wonders God had done among the nations through dem.
After dem were silent, James answer, “Brothers, listen to me.
Simeon has reported how God first visited the nations, to take out of dem a people for his name.
This agrees with the words of the prophets. As it is written,
‘After these things I go return. I go again build the tabernacle of David, which has fallen. I go again build its ruins. I go set it up,
That the rest of men may seek after the Lord; all the Gentiles Wey be call by my name, says the Lord, wey do all these things.
All of God’s works are known to him from eternity.’
“So my judgment is that we no trouble those from among the Gentiles who turn to God,
but that we write to dem that dem abstain from the pollution of idols, from sexual immorality, from Wetin be strangled, and from blood.
For Moses from generations of old has in every city people wey preach him, being read in the synagogues every Sabbath.”

Then it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole assembly, to choose men out of dem company, and send dem to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas: Judas call Barsabbas, and Silas, chief men among the brothers.
Dem wrote these things by dem hand: “The apostles, the elders, and the brothers, to the brothers Wey be of the Gentiles in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia: greetings.
Because we have heard that some who go out from us have troubled you with words, unsettling una souls, saying, ‘You must be circumcised and keep the law,’ to whom we give no commandment;
it seemed good to us, having come to one accord, to choose out men and send dem to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul,
men who have risked dem lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
We have sent so Judas and Silas, who themselves will also tell you the same things by word of mouth.
For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us, to lay no greater burden on you than these necessary things:
that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols, from blood, from things strangled, and from sexual immorality, from which if you keep unaself, it Go be well with you. Farewell.”
So, when dem were sent off, dem come to Antioch. Having gathered the plenty people together, dem delivered the letter.
When dem had read it, dem rejoiced over the encouragement.
Judas and Silas, also being prophets themselves, encouraged the brothers with many words, and strengthened dem.
After dem had spent some time there, dem were sent back with greetings from the brothers to the apostles.
But Paul and Barnabas stayed in Antioch, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord, with many others also.
After some days Paul talk say to Barnabas, “Let’s return now and visit our brothers in every city in which we proclaimed the word of the Lord, to see how Dem be doing.”
Barnabas planned to take John, who was call Mark, with dem also.
But Paul didn’t think that it was a good idea to take with dem someone who had withdrawn from dem in Pamphylia, and didn’t go with dem to do the work.
Then the contention grew so sharp that dem separated from each other. Barnabas take Mark with him, and sailed away to Cyprus,
but Paul chose Silas, and go out, being commended by the brothers to the grace of God.
He go through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the assemblies.
He come to Derbe and Lystra: and see am, a certain disciple was there, named Timothy, the son of a Jewess who believe; but his father was a Greek.
The brothers who were at Lystra and Iconium give a good testimony about him.
Paul want to have him go out with him, and he take and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those parts; for dem all know that his father was a Greek.
As dem go on dem way through the cities, dem delivered the decrees to dem to keep which Bin dey ordained by the apostles and elders who were at Jerusalem.
So the assemblies were strengthened in the faith, and increased in number daily.
When dem had gone through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, dem were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia.
When dem had come opposite Mysia, dem tried to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit didn’t allow dem.
Passing by Mysia, dem come down to Troas.
A vision appeared to Paul in the night. There was a man of Macedonia standing, begging him, and saying, “Come over into Macedonia and help us.”
When he had seen the vision, sharp-sharp we sought to go out to Macedonia, concluding that the Lord had call us to preach the Better news to dem.
Setting sail so from Troas, we made a straight course to Samothrace, and the day following to Neapolis;
and from there to Philippi, which is a city of Macedonia, the foremost of the district, a Roman colony. We were staying some days in this city.
On the Sabbath day we go outside of the city by a riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and we sat down, and spoke to the women who had come together.
A certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, one who worshiped God, heard us; whose heart the Lord opened to listen to the things which were spoken by Paul.
When she and her household were baptized, she begged us, saying, “If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house, and stay.” So she persuaded us.
As we were going to prayer, a certain girl having a spirit of divination met us, who bring her masters much gain by fortune telling.
Following Paul and us, she cried out, “These men are workers of the Most High God, who proclaim to us a way of salvation!”
She was doing this for many days. But Paul, becoming greatly annoyed, turned and talk say to the spirit, “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her!” It come out that very hour.
But when her masters see that the hope of dem gain was gone, dem seized Paul and Silas, and dragged dem into the marketplace before the rulers.
When dem had bring dem to the magistrates, dem talk say, “These men, being Jews, are agitating our city,
and advocate customs which it No be lawful for us to accept or to observe, being Romans.”
The plenty people rose up together against dem, and the magistrates tore dem clothes off of dem, and commanded dem to be beaten with rods.
When dem had laid many stripes on dem, dem threw dem into prison, charging the jailer to keep dem safely,
who, having received such a command, threw dem into the inner prison, and secured dem feet in the stocks.
But about midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to dem.
Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken; and sharp-sharp all the doors were opened, and everyone’s bonds were loosened.
The jailer, being roused out of sleep and seeing the prison doors open, drew his sword and was about to kill imself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped.
But Paul cried with a loud voice, saying, “No harm yourself, for We be all here!”
He call for lights, sprang in, fell down trembling before Paul and Silas,
bring dem out, and talk say, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?”
Dem talk say, “Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and You go be saved, you and una household.”
Dem spoke the word of the Lord to him, and to all who were in his house.
He take dem the same hour of the night, and washed dem stripes, and was sharp-sharp baptized, he and all his household.
He bring dem up into his house, and set chop before dem, and rejoiced greatly, with all his household, having believe in God.
But when it was day, the magistrates sent the sergeants, saying, “Let those men go.”
The jailer reported these words to Paul, saying, “The magistrates have sent to let you go; now so come out, and go in peace.”

But Paul talk say to dem, “Dem have beaten us publicly, without a trial, men Wey be Romans, and have throw us into prison! Do dem now release us secretly? No, most certainly, but Make dem come themselves and bring us out!”
The sergeants reported these words to the magistrates, and dem were afraid when dem heard that dem were Romans,
and dem come and begged dem. When dem had bring dem out, dem ask dem to depart from the city.
Dem go out of the prison, and entered into Lydia’s house. When dem had seen the brothers, dem encouraged dem, and comot.
Now when dem had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, dem come to Thessalonica, where there was a Jewish synagogue.
Paul, as was his custom, go in to dem, and for three Sabbath days reasoned with dem from the Scriptures,
explaining and demonstrating that the Christ had to suffer and rise again from the dead, and saying, “This Jesus, whom I proclaim to you, is the Christ.”
Some of dem were persuaded, and joined Paul and Silas, of the devout Greeks Plenty people, and not a few of the chief women.
But the unpersuaded Jews take along some wicked men from the marketplace, and gathering a crowd, set the city in an uproar. Assaulting the house of Jason, dem sought to bring dem out to the people.
When dem didn’t find dem, dem dragged Jason and certain brothers before the rulers of the city, crying, “These who have turned the world upside down have come here also,
whom Jason has received. These all act contrary to the decrees of Caesar, saying that E get another king, Jesus!”
The plenty people and the rulers of the city were troubled when dem heard these things.
When dem had taken security from Jason and the rest, dem Make dem go.
The brothers sharp-sharp sent Paul and Silas away by night to Beroea. When dem arrived, dem go into the Jewish synagogue.
Now these were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that dem received the word with all readiness of mind, examining the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so.
Many of dem so believe; also of the prominent Greek women, and not a few men.
But when the Jews of Thessalonica had knowledge that the word of God was proclaimed by Paul at Beroea also, dem come there likewise, agitating the plenty people.
Then the brothers sharp-sharp sent out Paul to go as far as to the sea, and Silas and Timothy still stayed there.
But people wey escorted Paul bring him as far as Athens. Receiving a commandment to Silas and Timothy that dem should come to him very sharp-sharp, dem comot.
Now while Paul waited for dem at Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he see the city full of idols.
So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons, and in the marketplace every day with people wey met him.

Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also were conversing with him. Some talk say, “What does this babbler want to say?” Others talk say, “He seems to be advocating foreign deities,” because he preached Jesus and the resurrection.
Dem take hold of him, and bring him to the Areopagus, saying, “May we know what this new teaching is, which is spoken by you?
For you bring certain strange things to our ears. We want to know so what these things mean.”
Now all the Athenians and the strangers living there spent dem time in nothing else, but either to tell or to hear some new thing.
Paul stood in the middle of the Areopagus, and talk say, “You men of Athens, I perceive that You be very religious in all things.
For as I passed along, and observed the objects of una worship, I find also an altar with this inscription: ‘TO AN UNKNOWN GOD.’ What so you worship in ignorance, this I announce to you.
The God who made the world and all things in it, he, being Lord of heaven and earth, no dey live in temples made with hands,
neither is he served by men’s hands, as though he needed anything, seeing he imself gives to all life and breath, and all things.
He made from one blood every nation of men to live on all the surface of the earth, having determined appointed seasons, and the boundaries of dem dwellings,
that dem should seek the Lord, if perhaps dem might reach out for him and find him, though he No be far from each one of us.
‘For in him we live, and move, and have our being.’ As some of una own poets have talk say, ‘For We be also his offspring.’
Being then the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the Divine Nature is like gold, or silver, or stone, engraved by art and design of man.
The times of ignorance so God overlooked. But now he commands that all people everywhere should repent,
because he has appointed a day in which he will judge the world in righteousness by the man whom he has ordained; of which he has given assurance to all men, in that he has raised him from the dead.”
Now when dem heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked; but others talk say, “We want to hear you again concerning this.”
Thus Paul go out from among dem.
But certain men joined with him, and believe, among whom also was Dionysius the Areopagite, and a woman named Damaris, and others with dem.
After these things Paul comot from Athens, and come to Corinth.

He find a certain Jew named Aquila, a man of Pontus by race, who had recently come from Italy, with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to depart from Rome. He come to dem,
and because he practiced the same trade, he lived with dem and worked, for by trade dem were tent makers.
He reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath, and persuaded Jews and Greeks.
But when Silas and Timothy come down from Macedonia, Paul was compelled by the Spirit, testifying to the Jews that Jesus was the Christ.
When dem opposed him and blasphemed, he shook out his clothing and talk say to dem, “Una blood be on una own heads! I be clean. From now on, I go go to the Gentiles!”
He comot there, and go into the house of a certain man named Justus, one who worshiped God, whose house was next door to the synagogue.
Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believe in the Lord with all his house. Many of the Corinthians, when dem heard, believe and were baptized.
The Lord talk say to Paul in the night by a vision, “No fear, but speak and no be silent;
for I be with you, and Nobody will attack you to harm you, for I have many people in this city.”
He lived there a year and six months, teaching the word of God among dem.
But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews with one accord rose up against Paul and bring him before the judgment seat,
saying, “This man persuades men to worship God contrary to the law.”
But when Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio talk say to the Jews, “If indeed it were a matter of wrong or of wicked crime, you Jews, it would be reasonable that I should bear with you;
but if Dem be questions about words and names and una own law, look to it unaself. For I no want to be a judge of these matters.”
So he drove dem from the judgment seat.
Then all the Greeks laid hold on Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him before the judgment seat. Gallio didn’t care about any of these things.
Paul, having stayed after this many more days, take his leave of the brothers, and sailed from there for Syria, together with Priscilla and Aquila. He shaved his head in Cenchreae, for he had a vow.
He come to Ephesus, and he left dem there; but he imself entered into the synagogue, and reasoned with the Jews.
When dem ask him to stay with dem a longer time, he declined;
but taking his leave of dem, and saying, “I must by all means keep this coming feast in Jerusalem, but I go return again to you if God wills,” he set sail from Ephesus.
When he had landed at Caesarea, he go up and greeted the assembly, and go down to Antioch.
Having spent some time there, he comot, and go through the region of Galatia, and Phrygia, in order, establishing all the disciples.
Now a certain Jew named Apollos, an Alexandrian by race, an eloquent man, come to Ephesus. He was mighty in the Scriptures.
This man Bin dey instructed in the way of the Lord; and being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, although he know only the baptism of John.
He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. But when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, dem take him aside, and explained to him the way of God more accurately.
When he had determined to pass over into Achaia, the brothers encouraged him, and wrote to the disciples to receive him. When he had come, he greatly helped people wey had believe through grace;
for he powerfully refuted the Jews, publicly showing by the Scriptures that Jesus was the Christ.
While Apollos was at Corinth, Paul, having passed through the upper country, come to Ephesus, and find certain disciples.
E tell dem say, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believe?” Dem tell am say, “No, we haven’t even heard that E get a Holy Spirit.”
He talk say, “Into what then were you baptized?” Dem talk say, “Into John’s baptism.”
Paul talk say, “John indeed baptized with the baptism of repentance, saying to the people that dem should believe in the one who would come after him, that is, in Jesus.”
When dem heard this, dem were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.
When Paul had laid his hands on dem, the Holy Spirit come on dem, and dem spoke with other languages and prophesied.
Dem were about twelve men in all.
He entered into the synagogue, and spoke boldly for a period of three months, reasoning and persuading about the things concerning God’s Kingdom.
But when some were hardened and disobedient, speaking evil of the Way before the plenty people, he comot from dem, and separated the disciples, reasoning daily in the school of Tyrannus.
This continued for two years, so that all people wey lived in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus, both Jews and Greeks.
God worked special miracles by the hands of Paul,
so that even handkerchiefs or aprons were carried away from his body to the sick, and the diseases comot from dem, and the evil spirits go out.
But some of the itinerant Jews, exorcists, take on themselves to invoke over people wey had the evil spirits the name of the Lord Jesus, saying, “We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preaches.”
There were seven sons of one Sceva, a Jewish chief priest, who did this.
The evil spirit answer, “Jesus I know, and Paul I know, but Wey be you?”
The man in whom the evil spirit was leaped on dem, and overpowered dem, and prevailed against dem, so that dem fled out of that house naked and wounded.
This became known to all, both Jews and Greeks, who lived at Ephesus. Fear fell on dem all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified.
Many also of people wey had believe come, confessing, and declaring dem deeds.
Many of people wey practiced magical arts bring dem books together and burned dem in the sight of all. Dem counted dem price, and find it to be fifty thousand pieces of silver.
So the word of the Lord was growing and becoming mighty.
Now after these things had ended, Paul determined in the spirit, when he had passed through Macedonia and Achaia, to go to Jerusalem, saying, “After I Don dey there, I must also see Rome.”
Having sent into Macedonia two of people wey served him, Timothy and Erastus, he imself stayed in Asia for a while.
About that time there arose no small stir concerning the Way.
For a certain man named Demetrius, a silversmith, who made silver shrines of Artemis, bring no little business to the craftsmen,
whom he gathered together, with the workmen of like occupation, and talk say, “Sirs, you know that by this business we have our wealth.
You see and hear, that not at Ephesus alone, but almost throughout all Asia, this Paul has persuaded and turned away many people, saying that Dem be no gods, that are made with hands.

Not only is there danger that this our trade come into disrepute, but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis Go be counted as nothing, and her majesty destroyed, whom all Asia and the world worships.”
When dem heard this dem were filled with anger, and cried out, saying, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”
The whole city was filled with confusion, and dem rushed with one accord into the theater, having seized Gaius and Aristarchus, men of Macedonia, Paul’s companions in travel.
When Paul want to enter in to the people, the disciples didn’t allow him.
Certain also of the Asiarchs, being his friends, sent to him and begged him not to venture into the theater.
Some so cried one thing, and some another, for the assembly was in confusion. Most of dem didn’t know why dem had come together.
Dem bring Alexander out of the plenty people, the Jews putting him forward. Alexander beckoned with his hand, and would have made a defense to the people.
But when dem perceived that he was a Jew, all with one voice for a time of about two hours cried out, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”

When the town clerk had quieted the plenty people, he talk say, “You men of Ephesus, what man is there who no dey know that the city of the Ephesians is temple keeper of the great goddess Artemis, and of the image which fell down from Zeus?
Seeing then that these things no fit be denied, you ought to be quiet, and to do nothing rash.
For you have bring these men here, Wey be neither robbers of temples nor blasphemers of una goddess.
If so Demetrius and the craftsmen Wey be with him have a matter against anyone, the courts are open, and E get proconsuls. Make dem press charges against each other.
But if you seek anything about other matters, it Go be settled in the regular assembly.
For indeed We be in danger of being accused concerning today’s riot, there being no cause. Concerning it, we wouldn’t be able to give an account of this commotion.”
When he had thus spoken, he dismissed the assembly.
After the uproar had ceased, Paul sent for the disciples, take leave of dem, and comot to go into Macedonia.
When he had gone through those parts, and had encouraged dem with many words, he come into Greece.
When he had spent three months there, and a plot was made against him by Jews as he was about to set sail for Syria, he determined to return through Macedonia.
These accompanied him as far as Asia: Sopater of Beroea; Aristarchus and Secundus of the Thessalonians; Gaius of Derbe; Timothy; and Tychicus and Trophimus of Asia.
But these had gone ahead, and were waiting for us at Troas.
We sailed away from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread, and come to dem at Troas in five days, where we stayed seven days.
On the first day of the week, when the disciples were gathered together to break bread, Paul talked with dem, intending to depart on the next day, and continued his speech until midnight.
There were many lights in the upper room where we were gathered together.

A certain young man named Eutychus sat in the window, weighed down with deep sleep. As Paul spoke still longer, being weighed down by his sleep, he fell down from the third floor, and was taken up dead.
Paul go down, and fell upon him, and embracing him talk say, “No be troubled, for his life is in him.”
When he had gone up, and had broken bread, and eaten, and had talked with dem a long while, even until break of day, he comot.
Dem bring the boy in alive, and were greatly comforted.
But we, going ahead to the ship, set sail for Assos, intending to take Paul aboard there; for he had so arranged, intending imself to go by land.
When he met us at Assos, we take him aboard, and come to Mitylene.
Sailing from there, we come the following day opposite Chios. The next day we touched at Samos and stayed at Trogyllium, and the day after we come to Miletus.
For Paul had determined to sail past Ephesus, that he might not have to spend time in Asia; for he was hastening, if it were possible for him, to be in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost.
From Miletus he sent to Ephesus, and call to imself the elders of the assembly.
When dem had come to him, E tell dem say, “You unaself know, from the first day that I set foot in Asia, how I was with you all the time,
serving the Lord with all humility, with many tears, and with trials which happened to me by the plots of the Jews;
how I didn’t shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable, teaching you publicly and from house to house,
testifying both to Jews and to Greeks repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus.
Now, see am, I go bound by the Spirit to Jerusalem, not knowing what will happen to me there;
except that the Holy Spirit testifies in every city, saying that bonds and afflictions wait for me.

But these things no count; nor do I hold my life dear to myself, so that I may finish my race with gladness, and the ministry which I received from the Lord Jesus, to fully testify to the Better news of the grace of God.
“Now, see am, I know that you all, among whom I go about preaching God’s Kingdom, will see my face no more.
So I testify to you today that I be clean from the blood of all men,
for I didn’t shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God.
Take heed, so, to unaself, and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to shepherd the assembly of the Lord and God which he purchased with his own blood.
For I know that after my departure, vicious wolves will enter in among you, not sparing the flock.
Men will arise from among una own selves, speaking perverse things, to draw away the disciples after dem.
So watch, remembering that for a period of three years I didn’t cease to admonish everyone night and day with tears.
Now, brothers, I entrust you to God, and to the word of his grace, which is able to build up, and to give you the inheritance among all people Wey sanctified.
I coveted Nobody’s silver, or gold, or clothing.
You unaself know that these hands served my necessities, and people wey were with me.
In all things I give you an example, that so laboring you ought to help the weak, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, that he imself talk say, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’”
When he had spoken these things, he knelt down and prayed with dem all.
Dem all wept a lot, and fell on Paul’s neck and kissed him,
sorrowing most of all because of the word which he had spoken, that dem should see his face no more. And dem accompanied him to the ship.
When we had comot from dem and had set sail, we come with a straight course to Cos, and the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara.
Having find a ship crossing over to Phoenicia, we go aboard, and set sail.
When we had come in sight of Cyprus, leaving it on the left hand, we sailed to Syria, and landed at Tyre, for there the ship was to unload her cargo.
Having find disciples, we stayed there seven days. These talk say to Paul through the Spirit, that he no suppose go up to Jerusalem.
When those days were over, we comot and go on our journey. Dem all, with wives and pikin dem, bring us on our way until we were out of the city. Kneeling down on the beach, we prayed.
After saying goodbye to each other, we go on board the ship, and dem come back home again.
When we had finished the voyage from Tyre, we arrived at Ptolemais. We greeted the brothers, and stayed with dem one day.
On the next day, we, who were Paul’s companions, comot, and come to Caesarea. We entered into the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, and stayed with him.
Now this man had four virgin daughters who prophesied.
As we stayed there some days, a certain prophet named Agabus come down from Judea.

Coming to us, and taking Paul’s belt, he bound his own feet and hands, and talk say, “Thus says the Holy Spirit: ‘So will the Jews at Jerusalem bind the man who owns this belt, and will deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles.’”
When we heard these things, both we and dem of that place begged him not to go up to Jerusalem.
Then Paul answer, “Wetin be you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I be ready not only to be bound, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.”
When he would not be persuaded, we ceased, saying, “The Lord’s Go be done.”
After these days we take up our baggage and go up to Jerusalem.
Some of the disciples from Caesarea also go with us, bringing one Mnason of Cyprus, an early disciple, with whom we would stay.
When we had come to Jerusalem, the brothers received us gladly.
The day following, Paul go in with us to James; and all the elders were present.
When he had greeted dem, he reported one by one the things which God had worked among the Gentiles through his ministry.
Dem, when dem heard it, glorified God. Dem tell am say, “You see, brother, how many thousands E get among the Jews of people wey have believe, and Dem be all zealous for the law.
Dem Don dey informed about you, that you teach all the Jews Wey be among the Gentiles to forsake Moses, telling dem not to circumcise dem pikin dem neither to walk after the customs.
What then? The assembly must certainly meet, for Dem go hear that you have come.
So do what we tell you. We have four men who have taken a vow.

Take dem, and purify yourself with dem, and pay dem expenses for dem, that dem may shave dem heads. Then all will know that E get no truth in the things that dem Don dey informed about you, but that you yourself also walk keeping the law.

But concerning the Gentiles who believe, we have written our decision that dem should observe no such thing, except that dem should keep themselves from chop offered to idols, from blood, from strangled things, and from sexual immorality.”
Then Paul take the men, and the next day, purified imself and go with dem into the temple, declaring the fulfillment of the days of purification, until the offering was offered for every one of dem.
When the seven days were almost completed, the Jews from Asia, when dem see him in the temple, stirred up all the plenty people and laid hands on him,

crying out, “Men of Israel, help! This is the man who teaches all men everywhere against the people, and the law, and this place. Moreover, he also bring Greeks into the temple, and has defiled this holy place!”
For dem had seen Trophimus, the Ephesian, with him in the city, and dem supposed that Paul had bring him into the temple.
All the city was moved, and the people ran together. Dem seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple. Sharp-sharp the doors were shut.
As dem were trying to kill him, news come up to the commanding officer of the regiment that all Jerusalem was in an uproar.
Sharp-sharp he take soldiers and centurions, and ran down to dem. Dem, when dem see the chief captain and the soldiers, stopped beating Paul.
Then the commanding officer come near, arrested him, commanded him to be bound with two chains, and inquired who he was and what he had done.
Some shouted one thing, and some another, among the crowd. When he no fit find out the truth because of the noise, he commanded him to be bring into the barracks.
When he come to the stairs, he was carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd;
for the plenty people of the people follow after, crying out, “Away with him!”
As Paul was about to be bring into the barracks, he ask the commanding officer, “May I speak to you?” He talk say, “Do you know Greek?
No be you then the Egyptian, who before these days stirred up to sedition and led out into the wilderness the four thousand men of the Assassins?”
But Paul talk say, “I be a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no insignificant city. I beg you, allow me to speak to the people.”
When he had given him permission, Paul, standing on the stairs, beckoned with his hand to the people. When there was a great silence, he spoke to dem in the Hebrew language, saying,
“Brothers and fathers, listen to the defense which I now make to you.”
When dem heard that he spoke to dem in the Hebrew language, dem were even more quiet. He talk say,

“I be indeed a Jew, born in Tarsus of Cilicia, but bring up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, instructed according to the strict tradition of the law of our fathers, being zealous for God, even as you all are today.
I persecuted this Way to the death, binding and delivering into prisons both men and women.

As also the high priest and all the council of the elders testify, from whom also I received letters to the brothers, and traveled to Damascus to bring dem also who were there to Jerusalem in bonds to be punished.
As I made my journey, and come close to Damascus, about noon, suddenly a great light shone around me from the sky.
I fell to the ground, and heard a voice saying to me, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?’
I answer, ‘Wey be you, Lord?’ He talk say to me, ‘I be Jesus of Nazareth, whom you persecute.’
“People wey were with me indeed see the light and were afraid, but dem didn’t understand the voice of him who spoke to me.
I talk say, ‘What shall I do, Lord?’ The Lord talk say to me, ‘Arise, and go into Damascus. There You go be told about all things which are appointed for you to do.’
When I no fit see for the glory of that light, being led by the hand of people wey were with me, I come into Damascus.
One Ananias, a devout man according to the law, well reported of by all the Jews who lived in Damascus,
come to me, and standing by me talk say to me, ‘Brother Saul, receive una sight!’ In that very hour I looked up at him.
He talk say, ‘The God of our fathers has appointed you to know his will, and to see the Righteous One, and to hear a voice from his mouth.
For You go be a witness for him to all men of Wetin you have seen and heard.
Now why do you wait? Arise, be baptized, and wash away una sins, calling on the name of the Lord.’
“When I had come back to Jerusalem, and while I prayed in the temple, I fell into a trance,
and see him saying to me, ‘Hurry and get out of Jerusalem sharp-sharp, because Dem go not receive testimony concerning me from you.’
I talk say, ‘Lord, dem themselves know that I imprisoned and beat in every synagogue people wey believe in you.
When the blood of Stephen, una witness, was shed, I also was standing by, and consenting to his death, and guarding the cloaks of people wey killed him.’
“He talk say to me, ‘Depart, for I go send you out far from here to the Gentiles.’”
Dem listened to him until he talk say that; then dem lifted up dem voice, and talk say, “Rid the earth of this fellow, for he no be fit to live!”
As dem cried out, and threw off dem cloaks, and threw dust into the air,
the commanding officer commanded him to be bring into the barracks, ordering him to be examined by scourging, that he might know for what crime dem shouted against him like that.
When dem had tied him up with thongs, Paul ask the centurion who stood by, “Is it lawful for you to scourge a man Wey be a Roman, and not find guilty?”
When the centurion heard it, he go to the commanding officer and told him, “Watch Wetin You be about to do, for this man is a Roman!”
The commanding officer come and ask him, “Tell me, are you a Roman?” He talk say, “Yes.”
The commanding officer answer, “I bought my citizenship for a great price.” Paul talk say, “But I was born a Roman.”
Sharp-sharp people wey were about to examine him comot from him, and the commanding officer also was afraid when he realized that he was a Roman, because he had bound him.

But on the next day, desiring to know the truth about why he was accused by the Jews, he freed him from the bonds, and commanded the chief priests and all the council to come together, and bring Paul down and set him before dem.
Paul, looking steadfastly at the council, talk say, “Brothers, I have lived before God in all good conscience until today.”
The high priest, Ananias, commanded people wey stood by him to strike him on the mouth.
Then Paul talk say to him, “God will strike you, you whitewashed wall! Do you sit to judge me according to the law, and command me to be struck contrary to the law?”
People wey stood by talk say, “Do you malign God’s high priest?”
Paul talk say, “I didn’t know, brothers, that he was high priest. For it is written, ‘You no go speak evil of a ruler of una people.’”

But when Paul perceived that the one part were Sadducees and the other Pharisees, he cried out in the council, “Men and brothers, I be a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. Concerning the hope and resurrection of the dead I be being judged!”
When he had talk say this, an argument arose between the Pharisees and Sadducees, and the crowd was divided.
For the Sadducees say that E get no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit; but the Pharisees confess all of these.

A great clamor arose, and some of the scribes of the Pharisees’ part stood up, and contended, saying, “We find no evil in this man. But if a spirit or angel has spoken to him, let’s not fight against God!”

When a great argument arose, the commanding officer, fearing that Paul would be torn in pieces by dem, commanded the soldiers to go down and take him by force from among dem, and bring him into the barracks.
The following night, the Lord stood by him, and talk say, “Cheer up, Paul, for as you have testified about me at Jerusalem, so you must testify also at Rome.”
When it was day, some of the Jews banded together, and bound themselves under a curse, saying that dem would neither eat nor drink until dem had killed Paul.
There were more than forty people who had made this conspiracy.
Dem come to the chief priests and the elders, and talk say, “We have bound ourselves under a great curse, to taste nothing until we have killed Paul.

Now so, you with the council inform the commanding officer that he should bring him down to you tomorrow, as though you were going to judge his case more exactly. We be ready to kill him before he comes near.”
But Paul’s sister’s son heard of dem lying in wait, and he come and entered into the barracks and told Paul.
Paul summoned one of the centurions, and talk say, “Bring this young man to the commanding officer, for he has something to tell him.”
So he take him, and bring him to the commanding officer, and talk say, “Paul, the prisoner, summoned me and ask me to bring this young man to you, who has something to tell you.”
The commanding officer take him by the hand, and going aside, ask him privately, “Wetin be it that you have to tell me?”
He talk say, “The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as though intending to inquire somewhat more accurately concerning him.

So no yield to dem, for more than forty men lie in wait for him, who have bound themselves under a curse neither to eat nor to drink until dem have killed him. Now Dem be ready, looking for the promise from you.”
So the commanding officer let the young man go, charging him, “Tell Nobody that you have revealed these things to me.”

He call to imself two of the centurions, and talk say, “Prepare two hundred soldiers to go as far as Caesarea, with seventy horsemen, and two hundred men armed with spears, at the third hour of the night.”
He ask dem to provide animals, that dem might set Paul on one, and bring him safely to Felix the governor.
He wrote a letter like this:
“Claudius Lysias to the most excellent governor Felix: Greetings.
“This man was seized by the Jews, and was about to be killed by dem, when I come with the soldiers and rescued him, having learned that he was a Roman.
Desiring to know the cause why dem accused him, I bring him down to dem council.
I find him to be accused about questions of dem law, but not to be charged with anything worthy of death or of imprisonment.
When I was told that the Jews lay in wait for the man, I sent him to you sharp-sharp, charging his accusers also to bring dem accusations against him before you. Farewell.”
So the soldiers, carrying out dem orders, take Paul and bring him by night to Antipatris.
But on the next day dem left the horsemen to go with him, and come back to the barracks.
When dem come to Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor, dem also presented Paul to him.
When the governor had read it, he ask what province he was from. When he understand that he was from Cilicia, he talk say,
“I go hear you fully when una accusers also arrive.” He commanded that he be kept in Herod’s palace.
After five days, the high priest, Ananias, come down with certain elders and an orator, one Tertullus. Dem informed the governor against Paul.
When he was call, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying, “Seeing that by you we enjoy much peace, and that prosperity is coming to this nation by una foresight,
we accept it in all ways and in all places, most excellent Felix, with all thankfulness.
But, that I no delay you, I entreat you to bear with us and hear a few words.
For we have find this man to be a plague, an instigator of insurrections among all the Jews throughout the world, and a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes.
He even tried to profane the temple, and we arrested him.
By examining him yourself you may ascertain all these things of which we accuse him.”
The Jews also joined in the attack, affirming that these things were so.
When the governor had beckoned to him to speak, Paul answer, “Because I know that you Don dey a judge of this nation for many years, I cheerfully make my defense,
seeing that you can recognize that it No be more than twelve days since I go up to worship at Jerusalem.
In the temple dem didn’t find me disputing with anyone or stirring up a crowd, either in the synagogues, or in the city.
Nor can dem prove to you the things of which dem now accuse me.
But this I confess to you, that after the Way, which dem call a sect, so I serve the God of our fathers, believing all things which are according to the law, and which are written in the prophets;
having hope toward God, which these also themselves look for, that there Go be a resurrection of the dead, both of the just and unjust.
For this matter I also practice always having a conscience void of offense toward God and men.
Now after some years, I come to bring gifts for the needy to my nation, and offerings;
amid which certain Jews from Asia find me purified in the temple, not with a mob, nor with turmoil.
Dem ought to Don dey here before you, and to make accusation, if dem had anything against me.
Or else let these men themselves say what injustice dem find in me when I stood before the council,
unless it is for this one thing that I cried standing among dem, ‘Concerning the resurrection of the dead I be being judged before you today!’”
But Felix, having more exact knowledge concerning the Way, deferred dem, saying, “When Lysias, the commanding officer, comes down, I go decide una case.”
He ordered the centurion that Paul should be kept in custody, and should have some privileges, and not to forbid any of his friends to serve him or to visit him.
But after some days, Felix come with Drusilla, his wife, who was a Jewess, and sent for Paul, and heard him concerning the faith in Christ Jesus.
As he reasoned about righteousness, self-control, and the judgment to come, Felix was terrified, and answer, “Go una way for this time, and when it is convenient for me, I go summon you.”
Meanwhile, he also hoped that money would be given to him by Paul, that he might release him. So also he sent for him more often, and talked with him.
But when two years were fulfilled, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus, and desiring to gain favor with the Jews, Felix left Paul in bonds.
Festus so, having come into the province, after three days go up to Jerusalem from Caesarea.
Then the high priest and the principal men of the Jews informed him against Paul, and dem begged him,
asking a favor against him, that he would summon him to Jerusalem; plotting to kill him on the way.
However Festus answer that Paul should be kept in custody at Caesarea, and that he imself was about to depart shortly.
“Make dem so”, talk say he, “that are in power among you go down with me, and if E get anything wrong in the man, Make dem accuse him.”
When he had stayed among dem more than ten days, he go down to Caesarea, and on the next day he sat on the judgment seat, and commanded Paul to be bring.
When he had come, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing against him many and grievous charges which dem could not prove,
while he talk say in his defense, “Neither against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar, have I sinned at all.”
But Festus, desiring to gain favor with the Jews, answer Paul and talk say, “Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem, and be judged by me there concerning these things?”
But Paul talk say, “I be standing before Caesar’s judgment seat, where I ought to be tried. I have done no wrong to the Jews, as you also know very well.

For if I have done wrong, and have committed anything worthy of death, I no refuse to die; but if none of those things is true that dem accuse me of, Nobody can give me up to dem. I appeal to Caesar!”
Then Festus, when he had conferred with the council, answer, “You have appealed to Caesar. To Caesar you shall go.”
Now when some days had passed, King Agrippa and Bernice arrived at Caesarea, and greeted Festus.
As he stayed there many days, Festus laid Paul’s case before the king, saying, “E get a certain man left a prisoner by Felix;
about whom, when I was at Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews informed me, asking for a sentence against him.

To whom I answer that it No be the custom of the Romans to give up any man to destruction, before the accused has met the accusers face to face, and has had opportunity to make his defense concerning the matter laid against him.
When so dem had come together here, I didn’t delay, but on the next day sat on the judgment seat, and commanded the man to be bring.
Concerning whom, when the accusers stood up, dem bring no charge of such things as I supposed;
but had certain questions against him about dem own religion, and about one Jesus, who was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive.
Being perplexed how to inquire concerning these things, I ask whether he was willing to go to Jerusalem and there be judged concerning these matters.
But when Paul had appealed to be kept for the decision of the emperor, I commanded him to be kept until I could send him to Caesar.”
Agrippa talk say to Festus, “I also would like to hear the man myself.” “Tomorrow,” he talk say, “you shall hear him.”

So on the next day, when Agrippa and Bernice had come with great pomp, and dem had entered into the place of hearing with the commanding officers and the principal men of the city, at the command of Festus, Paul was bring in.

Festus talk say, “King Agrippa, and all men Wey be here present with us, you see this man, about whom all the plenty people of the Jews petitioned me, both at Jerusalem and here, crying that he ought not to live any longer.
But when I find that he had committed nothing worthy of death, and as he imself appealed to the emperor I determined to send him,
of whom I have no certain thing to write to my lord. So I have bring him out before you, and especially before you, King Agrippa, that, after examination, I may have something to write.
For it seems to me unreasonable, in sending a prisoner, not to also specify the charges against him.”
Agrippa talk say to Paul, “You may speak for yourself.” Then Paul stretched out his hand, and made his defense.
“I think myself happy, King Agrippa, that I be to make my defense before you today concerning all the things that I be accused by the Jews,
especially because You be expert in all customs and questions which are among the Jews. So I beg you to hear me patiently.
“Indeed, all the Jews know my way of life from my youth up, which was from the beginning among my own nation and at Jerusalem;
having known me from the first, if Dem be willing to testify, that after the strictest sect of our religion I lived a Pharisee.
Now I stand here to be judged for the hope of the promise made by God to our fathers,
which our twelve tribes, earnestly serving night and day, hope to attain. Concerning this hope I be accused by the Jews, King Agrippa!
Why is it judged incredible with you, if God does raise the dead?
“I myself most certainly thought that I ought to do many things contrary to the name of Jesus of Nazareth.
This I also did in Jerusalem. I both shut up many of the saints in prisons, having received authority from the chief priests, and when dem were put to death I give my vote against dem.
Punishing dem often in all the synagogues, I tried to make dem blaspheme. Being exceedingly enraged against dem, I persecuted dem even to foreign cities.
“Whereupon as I traveled to Damascus with the authority and commission from the chief priests,
at noon, O king, I see on the way a light from the sky, brighter than the sun, shining around me and people wey traveled with me.
When we had all fallen to the earth, I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.’
“I talk say, ‘Wey be you, Lord?’ “He talk say, ‘I be Jesus, whom You be persecuting.

But arise, and stand on una feet, for I have appeared to you for this purpose: to appoint you a worker and a witness both of the things which you have seen, and of the things which I go reveal to you;
delivering you from the people, and from the Gentiles, to whom I send you,
to open dem eyes, that dem may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that dem may receive remission of sins and an inheritance among people Wey sanctified by faith in me.’
“So, King Agrippa, I No be disobedient to the heavenly vision,
but declared first to dem of Damascus, at Jerusalem, and throughout all the country of Judea, and also to the Gentiles, that dem should repent and turn to God, doing works worthy of repentance.
For this reason the Jews seized me in the temple, and tried to kill me.
Having so obtained the help that is from God, I stand to this day testifying both to small and great, saying nothing but what the prophets and Moses talk say would happen,
how the Christ must suffer, and how, by the resurrection of the dead, he would be first to proclaim light both to these people and to the Gentiles.”
As he thus made his defense, Festus talk say with a loud voice, “Paul, You be crazy! Una great learning is driving you insane!”
But he talk say, “I be not crazy, most excellent Festus, but boldly declare words of truth and reasonableness.
For the king knows of these things, to whom also I speak freely. For I be persuaded that none of these things is hidden from him, for this has not been done in a corner.
King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe.”
Agrippa talk say to Paul, “With a little persuasion are you trying to make me a Christian?”
Paul talk say, “I pray to God, that whether with little or with much, not only you, but also all that hear me today, might become such as I be, except for these bonds.”
The king rose up with the governor, and Bernice, and people wey sat with dem.
When dem had withdrawn, dem spoke to each other, saying, “This man does nothing worthy of death or of bonds.”
Agrippa talk say to Festus, “This man might Don dey set free if he had not appealed to Caesar.”
When it was determined that we should sail for Italy, dem delivered Paul and certain other prisoners to a centurion named Julius, of the Augustan band.
Embarking in a ship of Adramyttium, which was about to sail to places on the coast of Asia, we put to sea; Aristarchus, a Macedonian of Thessalonica, being with us.
The next day, we touched at Sidon. Julius treated Paul kindly, and give him permission to go to his friends and refresh imself.
Putting to sea from there, we sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were contrary.
When we had sailed across the sea which is off Cilicia and Pamphylia, we come to Myra, a city of Lycia.
There the centurion find a ship of Alexandria sailing for Italy, and he put us on board.
When we had sailed slowly many days, and had come with difficulty opposite Cnidus, the wind not allowing us further, we sailed under the lee of Crete, opposite Salmone.
With difficulty sailing along it we come to a certain place call Fair Havens, near the city of Lasea.
When much time had passed and the voyage was now dangerous, because the Fast had now already gone by, Paul admonished dem,
and talk say to dem, “Sirs, I perceive that the voyage Go be with injury and much loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of our lives.”
But the centurion give more heed to the master and to the owner of the ship than to those things which were spoken by Paul.

Because the haven No be suitable to winter in, the majority advised going to sea from there, if by any means dem could reach Phoenix, and winter there, which is a port of Crete, looking northeast and southeast.
When the south wind blew softly, supposing that dem had obtained dem purpose, dem weighed anchor and sailed along Crete, close to shore.
But before long, a stormy wind beat down from shore, which is call Euroclydon.
When the ship was caught, and no fit face the wind, we give way to it, and were driven along.
Running under the lee of a small island call Clauda, we were able, with difficulty, to secure the boat.
After dem had hoisted it up, dem used cables to help reinforce the ship. Fearing that dem would run aground on the Syrtis sand bars, dem lowered the sea anchor, and so were driven along.
As we labored exceedingly with the storm, the next day dem began to throw things overboard.
On the third day, dem threw out the ship’s tackle with dem own hands.
When neither sun nor stars shone on us for many days, and no small storm pressed on us, all hope that we would be saved was now taken away.
When dem Bin dey long without chop, Paul stood up in the middle of dem, and talk say, “Sirs, you should have listened to me, and not have set sail from Crete, and have gotten this injury and loss.
Now I exhort you to cheer up, for there Go be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship.
For there stood by me this night an angel, belonging to the God whose I be and whom I serve,
saying, ‘No fear, Paul. You must stand before Caesar. See am, God has granted you all people wey sail with you.’
So, sirs, cheer up! For I believe God, that it Go be just as it Don dey spoken to me.
But we must run aground on a certain island.”
But when the fourteenth night had come, as we were driven back and forth in the Adriatic Sea, about midnight the sailors surmised that dem were drawing near to some land.
Dem take soundings, and find twenty fathoms. After a little while, dem take soundings again, and find fifteen fathoms.
Fearing that we would run aground on rocky ground, dem let go four anchors from the stern, and wished for daylight.
As the sailors were trying to flee out of the ship, and had lowered the boat into the sea, pretending that dem would lay out anchors from the bow,
Paul talk say to the centurion and to the soldiers, “Unless these stay in the ship, you no fit be saved.”
Then the soldiers cut away the ropes of the boat, and let it fall off.
While the day was coming on, Paul begged dem all to take some chop, saying, “Today is the fourteenth day that you wait and continue fasting, having taken nothing.
So I beg you to take some chop, for this is for una safety; for not a hair will perish from any of una heads.”
When he had talk say this, and had taken bread, he Thank God to God in the presence of all, and he broke it, and began to eat.
Then dem all cheered up, and dem also take chop.
In all, we were two hundred seventy-six souls on the ship.
When dem had eaten enough, dem lightened the ship, throwing out the wheat into the sea.
When it was day, dem didn’t recognize the land, but dem noticed a certain bay with a beach, and dem decided to try to drive the ship onto it.
Casting off the anchors, dem left dem in the sea, at the same time untying the rudder ropes. Hoisting up the foresail to the wind, dem made for the beach.
But coming to a place where two seas met, dem ran the vessel aground. The bow struck and remain immovable, but the stern began to break up by the violence of the waves.
The soldiers’ counsel was to kill the prisoners, so that none of dem would swim out and escape.
But the centurion, desiring to save Paul, stopped dem from dem purpose, and commanded that people wey could swim should throw themselves overboard first to go toward the land;
and the rest should follow, some on planks, and some on other things from the ship. So dem all escaped safely to the land.
When we had escaped, then dem learned that the island was call Malta.
The natives showed us uncommon kindness; for dem kindled a fire, and received us all, because of the present rain, and because of the cold.
But when Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and laid dem on the fire, a viper come out because of the heat, and fastened on his hand.
When the natives see the creature hanging from his hand, dem talk say to each other, “No doubt this man is a murderer, whom, though he has escaped from the sea, yet Justice has not allowed to live.”
However he shook off the creature into the fire, and no be harmed.

But dem expected that he would have swollen or fallen down dead suddenly, but when dem watched for a long time and see nothing bad happen to him, dem changed dem minds, and talk say that he was a god.
Now in the neighborhood of that place were lands belonging to the chief man of the island, named Publius, who received us, and courteously entertained us for three days.
The father of Publius lay sick of fever and dysentery. Paul entered in to him, prayed, and laying his hands on him, healed him.
Then when this was done, the rest also who had diseases in the island come, and were cured.
Dem also honored us with many honors, and when we sailed, dem put on board the things that we needed.
After three months, we set sail in a ship of Alexandria which had wintered in the island, whose sign was “The Twin Brothers.”
Touching at Syracuse, we stayed there three days.
From there we circled around and arrived at Rhegium. After one day, a south wind sprang up, and on the second day we come to Puteoli,
where we find brothers, and were entreated to stay with dem for seven days. So we come to Rome.
From there the brothers, when dem heard of us, come to meet us as far as The Market of Appius and The Three Taverns. When Paul see dem, he thanked God, and take courage.
When we entered into Rome, the centurion delivered the prisoners to the captain of the guard, but Paul was allowed to stay by imself with the soldier who guarded him.

After three days Paul call together people wey were the leaders of the Jews. When dem had come together, E tell dem say, “I, brothers, though I had done nothing against the people, or the customs of our fathers, still was delivered prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans,
who, when dem had examined me, desired to set me free, because there was no cause of death in me.
But when the Jews spoke against it, I was constrained to appeal to Caesar, not that I had anything about which to accuse my nation.
For this cause so I ask to see you and to speak with you. For because of the hope of Israel I be bound with this chain.”
Dem tell am say, “We neither received letters from Judea concerning you, nor did any of the brothers come here and report or speak any evil of you.
But we desire to hear from you Wetin you think. For, as concerning this sect, it is known to us that everywhere it is spoken against.”

When dem had appointed him a day, many people come to him at his lodging. He explained to dem, testifying about God’s Kingdom, and persuading dem concerning Jesus, both from the law of Moses and from the prophets, from morning until evening.
Some believe the things which were spoken, and some disbelieved.
When dem didn’t agree among themselves, dem comot after Paul had spoken one word, “The Holy Spirit spoke rightly through Isaiah, the prophet, to our fathers,
saying, ‘Go to this people, and say, in hearing, You go hear, but will in no way understand. In seeing, You go see, but will in no way perceive.

For this people’s heart has grown callous. Dem ears are dull of hearing. Dem eyes dem have closed. Lest dem should see with dem eyes, hear with dem ears, understand with dem heart, and would turn again, and I would heal dem.’
“Be it known so to you, that the salvation of God is sent to the nations, and Dem go listen.”
When he had talk say these words, the Jews comot, having a great dispute among themselves.
Paul stayed two whole years in his own rented house, and received all who were coming to him,
preaching God’s Kingdom, and teaching the things concerning the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness, without hindrance.
Paul, a worker of Jesus Christ, call to be an apostle, set apart for the Better news of God,
which he promised before through his prophets in the holy Scriptures,
concerning his Son, who was born of the offspring of David according to the flesh,
who was declared to be the Son of God with power, according to the Spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord,
through whom we received grace and apostleship, for obedience of faith among all the nations, for his name’s sake;
among whom You be also call to belong to Jesus Christ;
to all Wey be in Rome, beloved of God, call to be saints: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
First, I thank my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, that una faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world.
For God is my witness, whom I serve in my spirit in the Better news of his Son, how unceasingly I make mention of you always in my prayers,
requesting, if by any means now at last I may be prospered by the will of God to come to you.
For I long to see you, that I may impart to you some spiritual gift, to the end that you may be established;
that is, that I with you may be encouraged in you, each of us by the other’s faith, both yours and mine.
Now I no desire to have you unaware, brothers, that I often planned to come to you, and was hindered so far, that I might have some fruit among you also, even as among the rest of the Gentiles.
I be debtor both to Greeks and to foreigners, both to the wise and to the foolish.
So, as much as is in me, I be eager to preach the Better news to you also Wey be in Rome.
For I be not ashamed of the Better news of Christ, for it is the power of God for salvation for everyone wey believe; for the Jew first, and also for the Greek.
For in it is revealed God’s righteousness from faith to faith. As it is written, “But the righteous shall live by faith.”
For the serious anger of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who suppress the truth in unrighteousness,
because that which is known of God is revealed in dem, for God revealed it to dem.

For the invisible things of him since the creation of the world are clearly seen, being perceived through the things that are made, even his everlasting power and divinity; that dem may be without excuse.
Because, knowing God, dem didn’t glorify him as God, neither Thank God, but became vain in dem reasoning, and dem senseless heart was darkened.
Professing themselves to be wise, dem became fools,
and traded the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds, and four-footed animals, and creeping things.
So God also give dem up in the lusts of dem hearts to uncleanness, that dem bodies should be dishonored among themselves,
who exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, Wey be blessed forever. Amen.
For this reason, God give dem up to vile passions. For dem women changed the natural function into that which is against nature.

Likewise also the men, leaving the natural function of the woman, burned in dem lust toward each other, men doing Wetin be inappropriate with men, and receiving in themselves the due penalty of dem error.
Even as dem refused to have God in dem knowledge, God give dem up to a reprobate mind, to do those things which No be fitting;
being filled with all unrighteousness, sexual immorality, wickedness, covetousness, malice; full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, evil habits, secret slanderers,
backbiters, hateful to God, insolent, haughty, boastful, inventors of evil things, disobedient to parents,
without understanding, covenant breakers, without natural affection, unforgiving, unmerciful;
who, knowing the ordinance of God, that people wey practice such things are worthy of death, not only do the same, but also approve of people wey practice dem.
So You be without excuse, O man, Anybody wey You be who judge. For in that which you judge another, you condemn yourself. For you who judge practice the same things.
We know that the judgment of God is according to truth against people wey practice such things.
Do you think this, O man who judges people wey practice such things, and do the same, that You go escape the judgment of God?
Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, forbearance, and patience, not knowing that the goodness of God leads you to repentance?
But according to una hardness and unrepentant heart You be treasuring up for yourself serious anger in the day of serious anger, revelation, and of the righteous judgment of God;
who “will pay back to everyone according to dem works:”
to people wey by perseverance in well-doing seek for glory, honor, and incorruptibility, life wey no dey end;
but to people Wey self-seeking, and no obey the truth, but obey unrighteousness, Go be serious anger and indignation,
oppression and anguish, on every soul of man wey do evil, to the Jew first, and also to the Greek.
But glory, honor, and peace go to every man wey do good, to the Jew first, and also to the Greek.
For E get no partiality with God.
For as many as have sinned without law will also perish without the law. As many as have sinned under the law Go be judged by the law.
For it no be the hearers of the law Wey be righteous before God, but the doers of the law Go be justified
(for when Gentiles who no have the law do by nature the things of the law, these, not having the law, are a law to themselves,
in that dem show the work of the law written in dem hearts, dem conscience testifying with dem, and dem thoughts among themselves accusing or else excusing dem)
in the day when God will judge the secrets of men, according to my Better news, by Jesus Christ.
Indeed you bear the name of a Jew, and rest on the law, and glory in God,
and know his will, and approve the things that are excellent, being instructed out of the law,
and are confident that you yourself are a guide of the blind, a light to people Wey in darkness,
a corrector of the foolish, a teacher of babies, having in the law the form of knowledge and of the truth.
You so who teach another, no you teach yourself? You who preach that a man shouldn’t steal, do you steal?
You who say a man shouldn’t commit adultery. Do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you rob temples?
You who glory in the law, through una disobedience of the law do you dishonor God?
For “the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you,” just as it is written.
For circumcision indeed profits, if You be a doer of the law, but if You be a transgressor of the law, una circumcision has become uncircumcision.
If so the uncircumcised keep the ordinances of the law, no go his uncircumcision be accounted as circumcision?
No go the uncircumcision which is by nature, if it fulfills the law, judge you, who with the letter and circumcision are a transgressor of the law?
For he No be a Jew Wey be one outwardly, neither is that circumcision which is outward in the flesh;
but he is a Jew Wey be one inwardly, and circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit not in the letter; whose praise No be from men, but from God.
Then what advantage does the Jew have? Or Wetin be the profit of circumcision?
Much in every way! Because first of all, dem were entrusted with the revelations of God.
For what if some were without faith? Will dem lack of faith nullify the faithfulness of God?
May it never be! Yes, let God be find true, but every man a liar. As it is written, “That you might be justified in una words, and might prevail when you come into judgment.”
But if our unrighteousness commends the righteousness of God, what will we say? Is God unrighteous who inflicts serious anger? I speak like men do.
May it never be! For then how will God judge the world?
For if the truth of God through my lie abounded to his glory, why am I also still judged as a sinner?
Why not (as We be slanderously reported, and as some affirm that we say), “Make we do evil, that good may come?” People wey say so are justly condemned.
What then? Are we better than dem? No, in no way. For we previously warned both Jews and Greeks, that Dem be all under sin.
As it is written, “E get Nobody righteous; no, not one.
E get Nobody who understands. E get Nobody who seeks after God.
Dem have all turned aside. Dem have together become unprofitable. E get Nobody wey do good, no, not so much as one.”
“Dem throat is an open tomb. With dem tongues dem have used deceit.” “The poison of vipers is under dem lips”;
“whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness.”
“Dem feet are swift to shed blood.
Destruction and misery are in dem ways.
The way of peace, dem haven’t known.”
“E get no fear of God before dem eyes.”
Now we know that Anything wey things the law says, it speaks to people Wey under the law, that every mouth may be closed, and all the world may be bring under the judgment of God.
Because by the works of the law, no flesh Go be justified in his sight. For through the law comes the knowledge of sin.
But now apart from the law, a righteousness of God Don dey revealed, being testified by the law and the prophets;
even the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ to all and on all people wey believe. For E get no distinction,
for all have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God;
being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus;
whom God sent to be an atoning sacrifice, through faith in his blood, for a demonstration of his righteousness through the passing over of prior sins, in God’s forbearance;
to demonstrate his righteousness at this present time; that he might imself be just, and the justifier of him who has faith in Jesus.
Where then is the boasting? It is excluded. By what kind of law? Of works? No, but by a law of faith.
We maintain so that a man is justified by faith apart from the works of the law.
Or is God the God of Jews only? No be he the God of Gentiles also? Yes, of Gentiles also,
since indeed E get one God who will justify the circumcised by faith, and the uncircumcised through faith.
Do we then nullify the law through faith? May it never be! No, we establish the law.
What then will we say that Abraham, our forefather, has find according to the flesh?
For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not toward God.
For what does the Scripture say? “Abraham believe God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness.”
Now to him who works, the reward No be counted as grace, but as something owed.
But to him who no dey work, but believe in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is accounted for righteousness.
Even as David also pronounces blessing on the man to whom God counts righteousness apart from works,
“Blessed are dem whose iniquities are forgiven, whose sins are covered.
Blessed is the man whom the Lord will by no means charge with sin.”
Is this blessing then pronounced on the circumcised, or on the uncircumcised also? For we say that faith was accounted to Abraham for righteousness.
How then was it counted? When he was in circumcision, or in uncircumcision? Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision.

He received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith which he had while he was in uncircumcision, that he might be the father of all people wey believe, though dem might be in uncircumcision, that righteousness might also be accounted to dem.
He is the father of circumcision to people wey not only are of the circumcision, but who also walk in the steps of that faith of our father Abraham, which he had in uncircumcision.
For the promise to Abraham and to his offspring that he should be heir of the world no be through the law, but through the righteousness of faith.
For if people Wey of the law are heirs, faith is made void, and the promise is made of no effect.
For the law produces serious anger, for where E get no law, neither is there disobedience.

For this cause it is of faith, that it may be according to grace, to the end that the promise may be sure to all the offspring, not to that only which is of the law, but to that also which is of the faith of Abraham, Wey be the father of us all.
As it is written, “I have made you a father of many nations.” This is in the presence of him whom he believe: God, wey dey give life to the dead, and calls the things that No be, as though dem were.
Besides hope, Abraham in hope believe, to the end that he might become a father of many nations, according to that which Bin dey spoken, “So will una offspring be.”
Without being weakened in faith, he didn’t consider his own body, already having been worn out, (he being about a hundred years old), and the deadness of Sarah’s womb.
Yet, looking to the promise of God, he didn’t waver through unbelief, but grew strong through faith, giving glory to God,
and being fully assured that what he had promised, he was also able to perform.
So it also was “credited to him for righteousness.”
Now it No be written that it was accounted to him for his sake alone,
but for our sake also, to whom it Go be accounted, who believe in him who raised Jesus, our Lord, from the dead,
who was delivered up for our trespasses, and was raised for our justification.
Being so justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ;
through whom we also have our access by faith into this grace in which we stand. We glad well-well in hope of the glory of God.
Not only this, but we also glad well-well in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces perseverance;
and perseverance, proven character; and proven character, hope:
and hope no dey disappoint us, because God’s love Don dey poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us.
For while we were yet weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly.
For one will hardly die for a righteous man. Yet perhaps for a righteous person someone would even dare to die.
But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.
Much more then, being now justified by his blood, We go be saved from God’s serious anger through him.
For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, We go be saved by his life.
Not only so, but we also glad well-well in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received the reconciliation.
So as sin entered into the world through one man, and death through sin; and so death passed to all men, because all sinned.
For until the law, sin was in the world; but sin No be charged when E get no law.
Nevertheless death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those whose sins no be like Adam’s disobedience, Wey be a foreshadowing of him who was to come.
But the free gift no be like the trespass. For if by the trespass of the one the many died, much more did the grace of God, and the gift by the grace of the one man, Jesus Christ, abound to the many.
The gift is No be like through one who sinned: for the judgment come by one to condemnation, but the free gift come of many trespasses to justification.

For if by the trespass of the one, death reigned through the one; so much more will people wey receive the abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness reign in life through the one, Jesus Christ.
So then as through one trespass, all men were condemned; even so through one act of righteousness, all men were justified to life.
For as through the one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, even so through the obedience of the one, many Go be made righteous.
The law come in besides, that the trespass might abound; but where sin abounded, grace abounded more exceedingly;
that as sin reigned in death, even so grace might reign through righteousness to life wey no dey end through Jesus Christ our Lord.
What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?
